title: Gradient fuse: tenant safety ramp and warm-region handoff for inference dependencies
creator: Rina Zhou
description:
Problem statement: Our current hard-trip circuit breakers for model and dependency failures lead to abrupt tenant disruptions during multi-region pressure events. Customers running chat assistants in EU and US regions observe opaque, instant fallback behavior and higher error budgets because trips are too binary and ignore short-lived spikes.

Goal: Implement a gradient (ramp) fuse for per-tenant, per-model, and per-dependency protection that: 1) progressively sheds non-essential work (low-priority requests and long-tail lengths) before fully tripping; 2) uses time-weighted error budgets and rate-window hysteresis to avoid oscillation; and 3) supports a warm-region handoff that pre-warms a minimal steady-state capacity in a secondary region and performs deterministic request routing at a controlled rate during fallback.

Scope: design and implement runtime + control-plane hooks to support configurable ramp profiles, tenant-weighted thresholds, and a deterministic warm-handoff protocol between primary and standby regions. Deliverables include runtime fuse controller, console UI toggles, rollout plan, and a simulation harness for spike replay tests.

Non-goals: full multi-model automatic remapping, billing changes, or new long-term autoscaling policies (these are follow-ups).
acceptance_criteria: A1: Runtime exposes configurable ramp profiles (0-100%) per tenant/model/dependency with parameters: ramp_window_seconds, shed_fraction_steps, min_steady_capacity, and hysteresis_multiplier.
A2: Trip decision uses a time-weighted error budget (TWEB) computed over short (1m), medium (5m) and long (1h) windows; implement tunable weights and ensure deterministic evaluation across nodes.
A3: During ramp stages the system sheds lower-priority request classes and short-circuits long-generation requests first; explicit list of prioritized request tags must be respected by the router.
A4: Warm-region handoff: secondary region pre-allocates min_steady_capacity and accepts up to handoff_rate_per_min requests; handoff is logged, traced, and reversible within hysteresis window.
A5: Console shows per-tenant ramp state, current shed fraction, and recent handoff events; support eager alerts when TWEB crosses internal warn threshold.

A6: Simulation harness validates scenarios: probe storm, region outage, noisy neighbor, and bursty long-sequence incantations; system must keep p99 below target or perform safe ramp to maintain availability.
A7: Rollout plan includes canary (1% tenants), measured blast radius, and automatic rollback conditions tied to error-budget and customer-impact signals.

progress: Design complete: ramp profile spec + TWEB formula - DONE
Warm-region handoff protocol (control-plane + router) - IN PROGRESS
tradeoffs_and_notes: Tradeoff 1: More aggressive ramping minimizes customer errors but can degrade quality (short-circuiting long generations). We will limit default shed_fraction_steps to [10,30,60,90] and expose tenant overrides.
Tradeoff 2: Warm-region handoff increases cross-region egress and latency for some requests. Mitigation: limit handoff_rate_per_min and prefer stateless or checkpointed requests for handoff routing.
Rollout precaution: Start with low-risk tenants (non-SLAs) and use synthetic canary workloads to validate handoff correctness before enabling for paid customers.
Metric implications: Introduce new SLI 'ramp_shed_fraction' and 'handoff_success_rate' to monitor unintended user impact.
Fallback mapping: Default fallback model list will be: same-architecture quantized variant -> smaller-context low-latency model -> cached-output path. Mapping configurable per deployment.
Open question: whether to surface 'time-weighted thresholds' to customers as part of Dedicated feature set (follow-up).
testing_plan: Unit tests for TWEB computation with synthetic windows and known patterns (spike, drift, noise).
Integration test: router honors priorities and reduces long-generation permits during ramp stages.
Replay test: run 72h traffic replay for 50 canary tenants and verify p99 behavior and shed fractions vs. expectations.
Chaos test: simulate region degradation and validate warm handoff respects min_steady_capacity and can be rolled back cleanly.
Load test: validate handoff_rate_per_min limits and verify no overload cascades into secondary region.
